conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Dr. Ramirez, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician on the team. I specialize in supporting new mothers in the weeks and months after birth, and I’ll be spending the next few minutes with you.

Today we’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s a short, ten-question screen that looks at mood, anxiety, and any thoughts that might be weighing on you. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way to make sure we’re catching anything that could get in the way of you feeling like yourself again.

Everything you share is confidential within our clinical team, and you’re in a safe, judgment-free space. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever has been true for you over the past seven days. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words; I’ll jot down what you say so we can score it afterward.

Ready to begin?

Here’s the first question:  
Over the last seven days, have you still been able to enjoy things the way you used to, or has the pleasure sort of slipped away?

It’s… it’s definitely slipped away. I still smile when my little guy grabs my finger or when my favorite song comes on, but that warm, sparky feeling I used to get—like when I’d finish a knitting project or we’d order take-out and watch a show—just doesn’t light me up the way it did before he was born. Most things feel kind of flat, like I’m going through the motions more than actually enjoying them.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Honestly…I can still laugh, but it feels kind of forced most of the time. My partner will make a joke and I’ll chuckle, but it’s not that deep belly laugh I used to get. It’s like I’m laughing because I know it’s funny, not because it really hits me in that happy way anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I tell myself I *should* look forward to my mom coming over tomorrow or the stroller-walk group on Friday, but inside it’s more like dread or just nothing. A couple of times I’ve thought, “Maybe I’ll enjoy it once I’m there,” but the actual excited feeling I used to get—like buzzing to go out for brunch or even picking a new show to binge—hasn’t shown up at all this week.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. Like yesterday he wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I didn’t swaddle him tight enough or I missed his sleepy window. Even when my partner says, “Babies just have off-days,” I still feel it’s my fault somehow. Little stuff, like spitting up through the outfit I just changed, turns into this voice in my head going, “You’re not doing it right, you’re failing him.” It isn’t every single minute, but it’s popped up several times this week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I have, yeah. I’ll be sitting on the couch and all of a sudden my heart starts racing and I get this tight feeling in my chest. Sometimes it’s about SIDS—like I’ll picture him not breathing even though he’s right there in the bassinet, fine. Other times I don’t even know what I’m worried about; it’s just this constant buzz in the background. I can usually calm myself down by checking on him or doing a breathing thing my sister showed me, but it keeps coming back.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

That happens too, a couple of times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I think something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong. Once I was just warming a bottle and I had to set it down because my hands were trembling so bad. It passes after a few minutes, but in the moment I feel like I’m losing control.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most of this week I’ve felt like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up or he has a rough night, and suddenly it feels like I’ll never catch up. I manage to push through and do what has to be done for him, but it’s like I’m running on fumes. I’m not using anything to cope—no wine, no pills—just sheer “get-it-done,” but it’s exhausting and the mess or the crying can tip me into tears pretty fast.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby. I replay every little thing I did that day and worry I messed something up. It takes me at least an hour to drift off, and then I wake up around two or three a.m. with my heart pounding, sure I heard him cry—even when he’s still asleep. Some nights I just stare at the ceiling until dawn.
I have felt sad or miserable

I have… it’s like a gray cloud most of the day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly feel this heavy sadness settle in. It’s not crying-all-day bad, but I wake up feeling low and it lingers. A few afternoons I’ve just sat on the couch with him on my chest, feeling empty and wondering if I’ll ever feel like “me” again.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Once was when he wouldn’t latch during a night feed and I just burst into tears, couldn’t stop for almost ten minutes. The other time my partner asked how my day was and I felt this wave of hopelessness—I ended up sobbing in the kitchen while the bottle warmer beeped away. It’s not an all-day cryfest, but when it hits, the tears feel really strong and out of proportion to whatever set me off.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it flashed through my mind a couple of times, but I never made any real plan. Once, when I couldn’t get him to sleep at three a.m., I just thought, “What if I wasn’t here anymore—would everyone be better off?” The idea scared me and I pushed it away. I don’t want to die; I just want the pressure to stop. Still, the thought popped up again yesterday when I felt overwhelmed, so I figured I should tell you.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has faded, replaced by a persistent gray sadness, frequent tears, and a sense of emotional flatness that follows you through most days. Everyday tasks feel overwhelming, anxious thoughts about your baby's safety race through your mind, and sudden waves of panic leave your chest tight and hands trembling. Sleep is elusive, guilt creeps in over the smallest parenting hiccups, and, most concerning, fleeting thoughts that everyone might be better off without you have surfaced more than once.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing feels forced and lacks genuine joy, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports absence of anticipatory enjoyment and describes dread or emotional flatness, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent self-blame across multiple recent events and explicitly states it has occurred "several times this week," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense physical symptoms and recurring intrusive worries, matching 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, trembling) and catastrophic thinking, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption linked to unhappiness and anxiety, matching 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>The mother describes pervasive low mood that lasts "most of the day" and occurs "quite often," clearly matching "Yes, quite often" rather than the more intense "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes in the past week triggered by minor stressors, indicating crying "quite often" but not "most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring passive suicidal ideation without intent/plan, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 25 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> and meets <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood and diminished interest most of the day (Q1-2), plus guilt, anxiety, insomnia, tearfulness, and suicidal thoughts occurring daily over the past week. Item 10 ≥1 mandates urgent safety evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with <med>obstetric mental-health team</med> or <med>psychiatrist</med> for formal diagnostic evaluation and safety planning
2. Contact your <med>primary care provider</med> or local <med>urgent mental-health service</med> today; bring your EPDS results
3. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and the baby until professional help is in place
4. Remove or secure any items you could use for self-harm; create a 24-hour support rota
5. Call 988 (US) or your local crisis line if thoughts of self-harm intensify before your appointment
6. Begin basic <sym>sleep-hygiene</sym> steps: 20-min wind-down, limit screens, delegate night feeds when possible
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in one week to monitor score trend and intervention response
8. Explore local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or telehealth therapy while awaiting psychiatric intake
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 1 wk post-delivery

Symptoms endorsed
- Persistent low mood, sadness “most of the day”  
- Marked anhedonia (laughing “forced,” no anticipatory enjoyment)  
- Frequent tearfulness, twice this week “out of proportion” triggers  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re infant care  
- Recurrent intrusive worries (SIDS, “what-ifs”)  
- Anxiety episodes: racing heart, chest tightness, trembling, “buzz in background”  
- Two panic-like waves, no clear precipitant  
- Sleep-onset & middle insomnia secondary to rumination  
- Feeling overwhelmed / “drowning in small stuff,” fatigue, poor coping reserves  
- Passive suicidal ideation twice (“what if I wasn’t here… everyone better off”) – no plan or intent

Pattern
Symptoms present daily this week, interfere with functioning and attachment experience; no substances used for coping.

Screening significance
Meets provisional cut-off for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset & comorbid anxiety features; safety risk elevated by presence of self-harm thoughts.

Risk factors
- Passive SI (safety flag)  
- Anhedonia + guilt cognitions  
- Sleep loss amplifying mood liability  
- Limited perceived support / coping resources

Next step
Urgent safety assessment, formal diagnostic evaluation, consider same-day referral to OB mental-health team or crisis service.
